According to Matthew, after the New Testament was given on the mountain, here he is first introduced as healed by the Lord, so that he who was shut out from the law, presuming that he is to be cleansed by the Lord’s power, might show that grace is not from the law but above the law, by which the leper could wash away his stain.
57_marg412: Like a humble man, blushing at the stains of his life, and not holding back his confession for shame, but, his wound laid bare, seeking a remedy.
57_interl466: he heals in the manner in which he is entreated: “Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean”
57_interl467: Bede. Ambrose. He grants power to the will, and does not doubt as an unbeliever, but, being conscious of his own defilement, does not presume.
57_marg413: Ambrose. Bede. As authority of power is shown in the Lord, so in this man the steadfastness of faith is declared.
57_interl468: Bede. Not that he could not heal without touch, but to show that he is not subject to the law.
57_marg414: Because of humility, to teach us to despise no one for any bodily stain. He touches, not disdaining; he commands, not distrusting; he applies the testimony of the work. “I will,” he says against Photinus; he commands against Arius; he touches against Manichaeus.
57_marg415: Bede. He touched, not that he could not heal without touch, but to show that he is not subject to the law, displaying himself as the lord of the law, who does not fear contagion.
57_interl471: in this, the power of majesty
57_interl472: “For he spoke, and they were made.”
57_interl473: Ambrose. Nothing lies between command and work, because the work is in the command.
57_marg416: And immediately the leprosy, etc. Ambrose. On this place: you see that it cannot be doubted that the will of God is power.
57_marg417: Where the leper is cleansed, the place is not named, so that it may be shown that not one people of some particular city, but all peoples, were healed.
57_marg418: Typically. The leper signifies the human race, full of leprosy, which, when the hand is stretched out, that is, when by the word of God it touches human nature, is cleansed from the variety of ancient error, so that, long abominable and set apart, it may now be able to be restored to the temple: “The temple of God is holy, which you are.” And be offered to the priest, of whom it is said: “Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech.” And let them offer for cleansing “your bodies a living host, holy, pleasing unto God.”
57_interl474: it was not necessary for him to boast in speech what he displayed in body
57_marg419: Bede. He orders silence, yet it cannot be silenced. Not that he wished something and was unable, but he gives an example: that his own people, in the great deeds they do, may wish to lie hidden, yet be revealed against their will so that they may profit others.
57_marg420: It teaches that our benefits are not to be published but kept back, so that we abstain not only from taking money for them but also from taking grace as a reward. Avoiding boasting makes it so that leprosy cannot pass over into the physician. Therefore silence is also commanded, because he thought better of those who believed with a more spontaneous faith than of those who believed for hoped-for benefits.
57_interl475: he sends him to the priests, because of humility, and so that, seeing, they may believe him, or, not believing, may be without excuse
57_marg421: Bede. So that the priest might understand that he was cleansed not by the order of the law but by the grace of God. “Offer”: he does not dissolve the law but fulfils it, he who walks according to the law; he seems to heal above the law those whom the remedies of the law had not healed. “As Moses commanded.” The law is spiritual, therefore it seems to have commanded a spiritual sacrifice, so that it may be a testimony to them, if they believe God, if the leprosy of impiety departs.
57_interl476: signs ought not to be removed before the things signified come
57_interl477: for cleansing they offered a round loaf of bread, two turtledoves, and a sextarius of oil
57_marg422: Bede. The healing of one drives many crowds to the Lord. For that he himself, outwardly and inwardly, showed that he was healed, the benefit received he does not keep silent about, even though commanded. But as Mark says, having fulfilled the evangelical office: “But he being gone out, began to publish and to blaze abroad the word: so that he could not openly go into the city, but was without in desert places: and they flocked to him from all sides.”
57_marg423: And he prayed, etc. When he prays he shapes the contemplative life; when he heals, the active life.
57_marg424: He heals as God, he prays as man. In the city he works miracles, in the desert he prays, so that he may show teachings both active and contemplative, so that no one, for the care of a neighbour, leaves the love of God, or, for the love of God, though he be the higher, leaves the care of his neighbour.
57_marg425: He who withdraws into the desert and prays restrains the rising tumult of vices, and seeks within himself a certain desert with the Lord, so that, with that outward tumult ceased, he may speak silently with him through inward desires.
57_marg426: And it came to pass, etc. Bede. Where he taught, sitting, Luke passed over for the sake of brevity. But Matthew says “into his own city,” and Mark “in Capharnaum”; this bears witness that he did this. But Galilee is called the city of Christ, in which were Nazareth and Capharnaum, to distinguish it from the transmarine region of the Gerasenes, from which he had crossed over and come into Galilee, as Matthew writes. Or Capharnaum itself is the city of Christ, which he made his own not by being born there, but by illustrating it with his powers.
57_marg427: Ambrose. Among the other remedies for the weak, with teachers coming from every side, this healing of the paralytic is described, as great and significant of a great matter. Whence it is said that he first prayed, not for the sake of help but to give an example, in which every sick person is taught to bring intercessors in seeking health, through whom the frame of our life, loosened, and the lame footsteps of our acts, may be reformed by the remedy of the heavenly word.
57_marg428: Allegorically. That is, raising up to higher things the minds of men, though numbed by the weakness of the outer man; by whose help the man is more easily placed, both to raise and to humble himself before Jesus, deserving to be seen by the Lord’s gaze. For God regards humility.
57_marg429: Bede. They desire to offer, but are shut out by the crowd standing between, because often the soul, looking toward God after the sluggishness of the sick body and desiring to be renewed by divine grace, is held back by the obstacle of its former way of life. Often, while it speaks with God in prayers, a crowd of thoughts coming in cuts off the sight of the mind, lest Christ be seen. But one must not remain outside among the lowest, where the crowds make their tumult, but must ascend to the roof of the house in which Christ teaches; that is, the height of holy Scripture is to be sought, and the law of God is to be meditated day and night, for by keeping his words the young man corrects his way. And the roof being opened, that is, the Scriptures unlocked, the sick man is let down, because by the piety of faith one descends to the humility of Christ and comes to the knowledge of Christ.
57_marg430: Bede. The house of Jesus is described as roofed with tiles, because under the contemptible veil of letters, if a teacher is present who unlocks them, the power of divine spiritual grace is found. Because he is let down with the bed, it signifies that Christ must be known by a man still placed in this flesh.
57_interl480: not of the paralytic, who lacked feeling
57_marg431: Bede. Each one’s own faith is worth much, since a man is saved inwardly and outwardly through another’s faith.
57_marg432: This healing of the paralytic signifies the salvation of a soul sighing toward God from the long-standing allurement of carnal sloth, which needs good teachers who may raise it up, offer it to Christ, and intercede for it. The four who are read in Mark to have carried him signify the four books of the gospels, or the four virtues by which, with trust, the mind is raised to deserve soundness: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice.
57_marg433: Man, your sins are forgiven, etc. You, a sinful man; I, God, who remit sins, forgive you your sins by the merit of others. Therefore let whoever is weighed down with sins take to himself the Church, which may pray for him.
57_marg434: Because the body was also weakened on account of the fault of the soul, therefore, about to heal the body, he first heals the soul.
57_marg435: Who can forgive, etc. No one forgives sins but God, who also forgives through those to whom he has given the power of forgiving. Therefore, since Christ forgives, he is proved to be truly God. They bear true testimony to God, but are deceived by denying the person of Christ. For perfidy can confess but cannot believe. Thus the testimony is not lacking to the divinity, but faith is lacking to salvation. God, wishing to save sinners, shows himself to be God both by knowledge of hidden things and by the wonder of his deeds, answering them: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” With the same majesty and power by which I see your thoughts, I can forgive men their offences. Understand from yourselves what the paralytic obtains. But because you do not know the spiritual grace, nor believe what was done inwardly, let it be proved by a visible sign that it is known to be no less power, so that you may know in the Son of man the hidden power of majesty by which he can forgive sins as God.
57_marg436: Ambrose. The great priest saw the leprosy in the hearts of the Jews, and shows them to be worse than that leper whom, once cleansed, he commanded to offer himself to the priest. But these the high priest rejects, lest their leprosy defile others also.
57_interl482: which only I know, who forgive
57_interl484: it hints at the resurrection of all
57_interl485: because the Son of man and God are the same
57_interl486: so that what was the proof of infirmity may be the proof of health
57_marg437: Bede. To rise is to draw the soul away from carnal desires. To take up the bed is to lift the flesh from earthly desires to the will of the spirit. To go home is to return to paradise, or to the inward keeping of oneself, lest it sin again.
57_marg438: Behold: by the remission of the penalty, understand the remission of the guilt.
57_interl487: lest, cured by the Christian faith, you remain in the unbelief of the Jews
57_interl488: Bede. Great is the power where salvation accompanies the command without delay; whence rightly those who were present, leaving off their blasphemies and astonished, are turned to the praise of so great majesty.
57_marg439: Ambrose. The unbelievers look on him as he rises, marvel at him as he departs, and prefer to fear the miracles of a divine work rather than to believe. For if they believed, they would not fear but would love: “Perfect charity casteth out fear.”
57_interl490: not so much with a bodily gaze as with the gaze of one who pities
57_interl491: Levi added or taken up, because divine election took him up and added him to the number of the apostles
57_marg440: Bede. The same Levi who is also Matthew. But Luke and Mark, out of honor to the evangelist, keep silent about the commonly known name. Matthew, however, at the beginning of his account, becoming his own accuser, names himself “Matthew the publican,” lest anyone despair of salvation because of the enormity of sins, since he was changed from publican to apostle, from tax collector to evangelist.
57_marg441: Ambrose. He left his own goods, who used to plunder the goods of others. He left not only the profits of the tolls, but also scorned the danger that could come from the rulers of the world, because he left the tax accounts unsettled. And because he reserved for himself no regard or thought for this life at all, he merited to be a faithful steward of the Lord’s talents.
57_marg442: Through the calling of Matthew is expressed the faith of the Gentiles, which before was greedy for worldly things, but now with devoted zeal refreshes the body of Christ. Through the pride of the Pharisees is hinted the envy of the Jews, which is tormented by the salvation of the Gentiles.
57_interl496: Ambrose. Not by the step of the body but by the affection of the mind.
57_interl497: not led by lightness but by the power of works and the divine power working within, he follows both in body and in mind
57_interl498: Bede. They had seen the publican turned from sins to better things, finding a place of penitence, and for this reason they too do not despair of salvation.
57_interl501: they err in two ways: they think themselves just when they are proud, and think those others guilty when they already repent
57_marg443: Ambrose. Every examination under the law that holds fast to justice has no mercy. All therefore have turned aside; but the Son of God, sent, tempered its severity by evangelical grace. He therefore calls sinners to penance, whose food and drink and walking and all that he did serve for salvation.
57_marg444: Bede. He who receives Christ into his inner dwelling is fed with the greatest delights of pleasures that overflow from within. Thus the Lord enters and reclines in the affection of him who believed. But again the envy of the faithless is kindled, and the likeness of future punishment is foreshadowed. For while the faithful feast and recline in the kingdom of heaven, the unbelief that fasts will be tormented. It is also shown how much difference there is between the rivals of the law and of grace, because those who follow the law will suffer an eternal hunger of the mind. But those who have received the Word in their inner selves, refreshed by the abundance of heavenly food and of the fountain, cannot hunger or thirst. And so those who fast in spirit murmur, saying: “Why with publicans, etc.” The sons of the devil spread the poison of the serpent. The serpent first uttered a voice to Eve, saying: What did God indeed say? “Eat not of every tree.” These men imitate him.
57_interl502: therefore I turn away from you, because you think you have no need
57_interl503: those who do not seek grace
57_marg445: Christ the physician, who by a wondrous kind of healing “was wounded for our iniquities.” By this remedy the poison of the serpent is driven out. He who uses this medicine does not remain fasting.
57_interl504: these I help, who by repenting give room to grace
57_interl505: who trust in their own righteousness
57_marg446: Bede. He calls the just those who, “not knowing the justice of God and seeking to establish their own, have not submitted themselves to the justice of God,” and, presuming on the law, do not seek the grace of the gospel. Sinners are those who, attending to their own evils, and not thinking they can be justified by the law, submit themselves to Christ’s grace by penitence.
57_marg447: Bede. Matthew says that the disciples themselves asked this. But it should be understood that both asked.
57_marg448: Spiritually the disciples of John and of the Pharisees fast, because whoever follows the works of the law or the traditions of men, or whoever hears the voice of Christ only with the ear, abstaining from good things, withers with a fasting heart. But whoever adheres to Christ is refreshed, because he feeds on his flesh and blood. John “drank neither wine nor strong drink,” because abstinence increases merit for him in whom there is no power of nature. But the Lord, who can forgive sins, why would he turn aside from sinners whom he could make more just than those who abstain? Christ also fasts, so that you may not decline the precept. He eats with sinners, so that you may understand grace and power.
57_marg449: Bede. Morally. As long as the bridegroom is with us and we are in gladness, we can neither fast nor mourn. But when he withdraws on account of sins, then a fast must be proclaimed and mourning must be taken up.
57_marg450: Bede. The bridegroom is Christ, the bride the Church. From this holy marriage the apostles were created through the bath of regeneration. Whence Mark calls them “the children of the marriage,” those who cannot mourn or fast as long as they see the bridegroom in the bridal chamber. And they know that he is with the bride; but when the wedding and the time of passion and resurrection have passed and the time has come, then the children of the bridegroom will fast, longing for the coming of the judge.
57_marg451: Bede. As if: you are going to make the mourners fast, since you are about to kill the bridegroom. This mourning for the absence of the bridegroom was observed not only after his death, but also before his incarnation, throughout the whole time of this age, when the saints desired the incarnation. But after the ascension the saints long for the coming of the judge. Nor did this mourning rest, except while the Lord lived in the flesh with his disciples.
57_interl512: from love of the world, not only from foods
57_marg452: He answers about both fasts, which are in tribulation or in joy. “When the bridegroom shall be taken away,” then they will be in grief and mourning until consolation is given through the Holy Ghost; and having received this gift, they will celebrate the fast that arises from joy, now renewed into spiritual life. And here he first treats of the fast that pertains to the humility of tribulation. But that which pertains to the joy of the mind, when the mind is lifted up to spiritual things and therefore is estranged from bodily foods, he signifies by the following similitudes, showing that this kind of fasting does not suit the carnal, who for this reason still draw in the old sense.
57_interl514: why the fast does not yet agree with the apostles
57_interl518: because it begins to displease, though it had pleased before
57_marg453: Bede. The disciples are compared to an old garment, for they are still the old man. A new patch, that is, some part of the new life, ought not to be put on them. If this is done, the new garment itself, that is, the teaching of the new life, is in a way torn: the part of it that is useful for fasting from foods is imparted untimely, since that teaching is a general fast, not only from the desire of foods but from all the joy of temporal delights. The part of that general fast which pertains to foods ought not to be imparted to men still given over to old custom, because there too a tearing seems to happen. And it does not suit that very oldness, because it is to be feared that through excessive austerity they lose even the faith they had, since the acts of the old and new man ought not to be mixed. For a garment of mixed colors does not please the bridegroom. Whence the Apostle: “stripping yourselves of the old man with his deeds, and putting on the new.”
57_interl522: the mysteries of the new life are not to be entrusted to minds not yet renewed
57_marg454: We are refreshed inwardly by wine, and clothed outwardly by a garment. The garments, therefore, are the good works which we do outwardly, by which we shine before men. The wine is the fervor of faith, hope and charity, by which in the sight of God we are reformed inwardly in newness of mind.
57_interl523: which, if it were done, neither untrained minds could bear it, and the teaching itself would do no good, and the minds themselves would be suffocated or crushed by the weight of sins
57_marg455: Bede. Old wineskins are also compared to those who are more easily burst by the spiritual precepts, the new wine, than they can contain them. New wineskins will be those who, after the ascension, having received the Spirit, will be renewed by praying for and hoping for his consolation. Otherwise: souls not yet renewed, but persevering in the old age of malice, ought not to be entrusted with the sacraments of new mysteries. [2] Otherwise: the old wineskins are the scribes and Pharisees. The new patch and the new wine are the precepts of the gospel, which the Jews cannot sustain, lest a greater tear be made; the Galatians mixed the precepts of the law with these, putting new wine into old wineskins. But they are fitting for the apostles, not for those who, corrupted by the traditions of their elders, cannot keep the sincerity of Christ’s precepts. Whence it is added: “And no man drinking old, hath presently a mind to new,” because the Jews, steeped in the flavor of the old life, found the precepts of the new grace distasteful, since, heaped up with their elders’ traditions, they could not perceive the sweetness of spiritual words.
57_interl524: let the new mysteries be entrusted to minds renewed
57_marg456: The frailty of the human condition is revealed when our bodies are compared to the cast-off skins of dead animals. But when the wineskins are renewed, new wines are stored, when we keep inviolate the sacraments we have received. If these skins are full, grace preserves them; if empty, moth and rust consume them. Therefore let them always be full.
57_interl525: the teaching is handed down to memory, and the mind is not without fruit
57_interl526: for it wills afterward if it is renewed, which also happened to the apostles
57_interl527: whether it is one word or two words
57_marg457: Bede. The day on which the letter of the sabbath had begun to be loosed he calls deuteron proteron, that is, second-first sabbath, hinting that the observance of the legal sabbath will cease, and the liberty of the natural sabbath, which up to the time of Moses was like the other days, is to be restored, by which believers, through the grace of the sevenfold Spirit, are free from evil works. The sabbath of grace, therefore, is called second-first in distinction from the legal sabbath: that is, first, placed second, that is, superior and more worthy than the lower legal. Or in order of time, because even before the law this sabbath was kept by the fathers as it is now kept by us. Or it can be called second-first, so that the one and the same sabbath of the New Testament is both second, because it is observed by us after the legal, and first, because it was observed by the just of old before the decrees of the law.
57_marg458: Literally: on another sabbath which after that one was first second; or which occurs first after the second, counting from that by which the preceding things were said or done.
57_marg459: Through the corn fields, etc. Mystically. The field is the world. The crop of the field is “the fruitfulness of the human race”; the ears, “the fruit of the Church,” with which the apostles are filled, nourishing themselves on our progress.
57_marg460: His disciples plucked the ears, etc. The disciples, not having room to eat because of the importunity of the crowds, were hungry like men; but by plucking the ears they comforted their want, which is a sign of a sterner life: they seek not prepared foods, but simple food. And note that the apostles now destroy the letter of the sabbath, against the Ebionites, who receive the other apostles but reject Paul as a transgressor of the law.
57_marg461: Mystically. Disciples hungry for the salvation of men pass through the cornfields, that is, through regions that are white for the harvest. “They rub the ears,” because in those whom they wish to bring into the body of Christ, they mortify the old man with his deeds, drawing him away from earthly intention, proposing examples of works, removing the coverings of the ears, and incorporating the cleansed grains into the members of the Church through the mouths of preachers. In Mark the disciples are reported to have done this while going before the Lord, because it is necessary that the teacher’s word precede, so that the heart of the hearer may be illumined by the grace of heavenly instruction. But the Jews think this is not lawful on the sabbath. Christ, by the gift of new grace, shows that the leisure of the law is a work of grace, rebuking the teachers of the law for not knowing the law.
57_marg462: Some of the Pharisees said to them, etc. Others say these things were objected to the Lord himself. But they could have been objected by different people both to the Lord and to the disciples, and whoever it was objected to, it refers chiefly to him.
57_interl528: according to the command of the law
57_marg463: On the sabbath days, etc. Sabbaths signify holy days of rest; or those that are kept in this age by those who devote themselves to the superstitions of the Jews; or those that will be kept in the future, when we eat the good things of the earth in perpetual solemnity.
57_marg464: Have you not read so much as this, etc. Bede. How is a crime imputed to the Lord which is not held as a crime in a servant? He is the true king and priest; and therefore the Lord of the sabbath is not held guilty of the harm of the ears plucked on the sabbath.
57_marg465: When David was hungry, etc. Bede. If David and Abimelech, through the excuse of hunger, are not rebuked for transgressing the command of the law, why do you not approve the same hunger in the apostles?
57_marg466: Allegorically. David, who fled with his companions from the face of Saul, signifies Christ, who with his disciples lies hidden from the prince of the world. David, the observer of the law, eats the consecrated bread and gives it to those who are with him, signifying the priestly food destined to pass to the use of the peoples; or because all the sons of the Church are priests, anointed by the Holy Ghost, that they may offer themselves.
57_marg467: How he went into the house of God, etc. The great grace of hospitality, with the danger of death placed before it: the mind of the priest does not decline the guest. And thus we ought to transfer others’ dangers onto ourselves. But also the true David, received by the hospitality of the mind, the priests do not exclude, not even for the danger of death.
57_interl530: is over, not under, the old observance, and therefore he who observes according to its observance does not sin
57_interl531: Bede. He teaches and cures especially on the sabbaths, not only to insinuate the spiritual sabbath but also for the more crowded assembly of the people.
57_marg468: Bede. Mystically. This man signifies the human race, dried up in the fruitfulness of good work, in place of the hand stretched out to the tree in the first parent, which the innocent hand, stretched out on the cross, heals. And rightly the hand in the Synagogue was withered, because where there is a greater gift of knowledge, there the transgressor lies under greater guilt.
57_marg469: Bede. Because the master excused by a plausible example the breaking of the sabbath which they charged against the disciples, now, by watching the master himself, they wish to slander him: so that if he does not heal, they may charge him with cruelty or weakness; if he does, they may charge him with transgression.
57_interl532: “The Lord knoweth the thoughts of men, that they are vain.”
57_marg470: Bede. Forestalling the slander they were preparing for him, he rebukes those who, by interpreting the precepts of the law badly, thought that even good works should be kept from on the sabbath, since the law commands abstaining from servile work, that is, from evil, on the sabbath. In this is signified that on the seventh rest those who did good in the six ages of this world will have their rest, not from good things, but from evil.
57_interl536: that is, to heal the man
57_marg471: Bede. He asks about the salvation of the soul while about to heal the body, because he was doing those miracles for the salvation of the soul, and this very healing of the hand signified the salvation of the soul. Or by the name of soul the whole man is signified.
57_interl537: that is, not to keep him safe from destruction
57_marg472: Bede. God is not the author of evil; but those whom he does not save are said to be destroyed.
57_interl538: as if angry at them, while they were silent
57_interl539: to the poor, that you may help your neighbor and bring the protection of a widow; stretch out to God, praying for your sins
57_marg473: Bede. The fruitless weakness of the soul is cured in no better way than by the largeness of almsgiving. Whence it is said: “Let not thy hand be stretched out to receive, and shut when thou shouldst give.” Because he stretches his hands out to God in vain, asking pardon for his sins, who does not stretch them out to the poor as far as he can.
57_interl540: which had withered by sin is watered with the saving juices of good works
57_interl541: because the miracle immediately follows God’s command
57_marg474: Because they were moved by spite alone: it was no fault either for a man to stretch out his hand or for Jesus to heal. It was great folly to plot the death of him whose benefits they greatly needed.
57_interl544: a form is prescribed which you ought to imitate
57_marg475: The mountain on which he chooses and teaches the apostles signifies the height of justice, because they were to be instructed and to preach, not to remain in the lowest, but to be lifted up to heights; so also the law was given on a mountain. He leads the apostles up more eminently, so that from the mountain they might first receive the mountains to announce peace to the people. Thus also Moses, alone understanding the law spiritually, ascended the peak of the mountain in which God was.
57_marg476: Morally. He who seeks God by praying advances to higher things; he ascends to the summit of the lofty court. But the Lord prays, not for himself as one powerless, but for me as one merciful. Whence it is immediately added: “And when day was come, he called unto him his disciples,” all who learn the way of the kingdom by his teaching.
57_marg477: Of whom he chose twelve, whom he named apostles, that is, sent in their place. Whence: “As the Father hath sent me, I also send you.” Ascending the mountain, he calls to himself and chooses whom he wills, because it is not for their zeal, but by divine grace, that they were called to the apostleship. Whence: “You have not chosen me: but I have chosen you.”
57_marg478: He chose men neither wise, nor rich, nor noble, lest he should seem to have led them by prudence, to have bought them with riches, or to have drawn anyone to grace by the authority of power and nobility.
57_interl546: so that they might mark the square world with the faith of the Trinity
57_marg479: Not only first, but long before, when he is said to have been brought by Andrew: “Thou shalt be called Cephas, which is interpreted Peter.” But Luke, wishing to name the twelve apostles, and having to name Peter, wished briefly to hint that he was not called this before, but that the Lord surnamed him thus, so that it might not be thought to have happened by chance, but that through the change the mystery of the rock might be commended to the hearers.
57_marg480: Matthew, out of humility, places himself in order below his fellow Thomas, although the other evangelists have placed him before him.
57_marg481: The Lord went up into the mountains to choose the apostles; to teach the crowds he came down again to the plains, because only in a humble place are the crowds able to see Christ; and it is rare to find either a crowd following the Lord to higher things, or someone sick being healed on the mountain. But with the fever of lusts quenched and the light of knowledge kindled, each one gradually climbs the summit of virtues.
57_marg482: Not from the nearby sea of Galilee, since they do not count this among the places of miracle, but it is named from the great sea. In it Tyre and Sidon also could be included. But because they are cities of the Gentiles, they are deliberately named one by one, so that the greatness of Christ’s power may be made known, which also stirs foreign cities.
57_marg483: If we say there were two sermons: he went up the mountain and had disciples there, and afterward came down and made that one to the crowd. If we say it was one, it must be understood thus: he went up the mountain, and after a little came down, and there gave the sermon where there was a plain.
57_marg484: He touches Christ who faithfully believes in him; he is touched by Christ who is strengthened in him. Whoever thus touches and is touched is healed in spirit by his power.
57_marg485: And he, lifting up his eyes, etc. Although he speaks generally to all, he lifts his eyes specially to the disciples, so that those who receive the word of God with the attentive ear of the heart may receive the fuller light of inner savor. While sitting on the mountain he opened his mouth to them, so that he might bring forth great things; standing in the plain he directs his eyes to them, that they may plainly understand what they have heard.
57_interl549: these abstain from sin, tread the world underfoot, and do not seek enticements
57_marg486: Those who cannot yet climb the citadel of perfect virtue are to be cherished in the meantime by the general blessedness of perfection, so that, gradually advancing to better things, while they willingly listen to the Lord standing on the plain, they may at some time rise up sublimely to him sitting on the mountain. For he addresses as standing those whose hearts he still tames; those whom he finds trained by long study and now docile, to these, as one resting seated, he expresses mystical things.
57_marg487: What in Matthew is said in full through the eight beatitudes, in the sermon of perfection to the apostles on the top of the mountain, in Luke is comprehended more temperately through four cardinal virtues, in a lighter sermon to the crowds below. He says therefore: “Blessed are the poor in spirit”: behold temperance, which also makes purity of heart. “Blessed are ye that hunger now”: those who suffer with others and show mercy and give their goods, not seeking what is others’: behold justice, which also makes mercy. “Blessed are ye that weep now”: behold prudence, which considers how wretched earthly things are and how blessed the heavenly, and which also makes peace. “Blessed shall you be when men shall hate you”: behold fortitude, which also makes gentleness. He is strong who conquers anger and the other movements of the mind. The virtues are linked, so that whoever has one seems to have many; but the reward is of the one that is richer, and richer the reward. The hospitality, humility and holiness of Abraham are commended; but because he excelled in faith, by faith he merited the principality above the rest.
57_marg488: He who hungers suffers with the hungry; by suffering with him he gives; by giving he becomes just; he makes himself equal to those below him, excludes deceit, and seeks truth.
57_interl552: from present misery, from the postponement of good things
57_marg489: Blessed are ye that weep now, etc. He who desires weeping, hunger and poverty for the sake of the riches of Christ’s inheritance, for the bread of eternal life, for the hope of heavenly joys, is blessed. Much more blessed is he who does not tremble to keep these virtues amid adversities.
57_interl554: by expelling them from the synagogues
57_interl556: as far as Jews and Gentiles are concerned, the Christian name is often erased from memory and cast out by men
57_interl559: many for those suffering on earth; there will be a great reward in heaven
57_marg490: Amid the hatreds of hearts, amid the reproaches of tongues, amid the hands of persecutors, live with a more joyful heart, looking to the heavenly reward.
57_interl560: who did not fail from the truth through fear
57_marg491: According to these things, etc. He strengthens them by the example of the prophets, because those who speak true things are wont to suffer persecution.
57_interl561: now indeed they can reproach and prevail, but for them: Woe
57_interl562: because you will lose the use of temporal goods, which you now love
57_interl563: against the necessary miseries of time
57_marg492: Matthew, on the mountain, describes only the beatitudes of the upright. But Luke, in the plain, also describes the “woes” of the wicked, because hearers who are still rude must be compelled to good things by threats and terrors; the perfect are enough invited by rewards.
57_marg493: Since it is said above that the poor belong to the kingdom of heaven, it appears from the opposite that he estranges himself from this kingdom who seeks consolation in temporal things. Nor is it riches so much as the love of riches that is blameworthy.
57_marg494: The rich man: ‘the Jewish people,’ or ‘the heretic,’ or ‘the philosopher of the world,’ who, delighted with an abundance of words and the patronage of eloquence, having passed beyond the simplicity of true faith, have stored up useless treasures, disputing about the generation of Christ according to the custom of the age. In the future they will recognize the poverty of their faith, and, worn down by eternal fasting, will know that the food of perfidy which they now belch up is the cause of so great a punishment. And there will be a time when they will mourn their laughter, to whom it is rightly said: “Woe to you when men shall bless you”; because while here they please the powerful, they subject themselves to a perpetual curse. For as the poor, the hungry and the weeping are proved in uprightness amid evils, so the rich, idle in riches, banquets and laughter, are cherished for a greater punishment by the evil clientele of their flatterers.
57_interl565: who, pleasing yourselves in your desires, suffer no hunger for true good
57_marg495: You who abound more among the rich, like “a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted,” who asks from the finger of Lazarus a drop of water.
57_marg496: Solomon: “The heart of the wise is where sadness is; the heart of fools is where joy is,” teaching that folly is to be ascribed to those who laugh, and prudence to those who weep.
57_marg497: A large part of sinners is nearly this: their crimes are not only not rebuked, but moreover praised as if they were well done.
57_interl567: that is, they blessed false prophets, who, to catch the favor of the crowd, prophesied from their own heart
57_marg498: Love your enemies, etc. Having said what they can suffer from enemies, he sets out how they ought to conduct themselves toward them; and here the Church is not steeped in milk but strengthened with the stronger food of charity. It is not enough not to hate; what is beyond human nature is commanded: to love. And when the law commands retaliation in return, the gospel gives charity for enmities, kindness for hatred, prayers for curses, patience for persecutors, and even the grace of reward to the hungry.
57_interl570: by ministering food to the mind, or even to the body
57_interl572: Hence the Apostle: “We are cursed, and we bless; we are blasphemed, and we entreat.”
57_marg499: What the prophets seem to call down as curses. These are not the wishes of those who desire, but foretellings of future things, for they themselves prayed for their enemies.
57_marg500: And he that strikes you, etc. Since charity is patient, it ought to endure the patience of the one who strikes. Since it is kind, it ought not to answer curses. If it seeketh not her own, it ought not to resist the one who seizes. If it envieth not, it ought not to hate the enemy.
57_interl574: Offer him. The physician of souls, whom he instructs to cure their neighbors, commands them to endure whatever can avail for the salvation of their neighbors. And it belongs to mercy that, as with sick and frantic sons, if their health demands it, they suffer much until the sickness passes. What is so wonderful as offering the cheek to one who strikes? Indeed every impulse of an indignant man is broken, anger is calmed, and through patience he is invited to penitence.
57_marg501: Cloak, etc. What is said of cloak and tunic is to be done also in other things which we say are ours by some temporal right. For if this is commanded of necessities, much more is it commanded to despise superfluities.
57_marg502: Because it is little not to do harm, it adds about benefits.
57_interl577: house, field, and generally whatever money
57_marg504: Ask them not again, etc. Because “charity is patient, is kind,” it not only bears firmly the injuries of an enemy, but also kindly anticipates the grace of a friend, so that they may be drawn by other benefits. Whence he instructs more widely by adding: “And if you love them.”
57_marg505: So that it may not seem to dissolve the law, it keeps the reciprocity in benefits, which it neglects in injuries. Nor does it say ‘as they do,’ but ‘as you wish that men do to you,’ and you do to them, so that the return may be fuller, and the deed may equal the wish.
57_marg506: And not only now extend works of charity to friends, but also to enemies, so that they may begin to be friends; first extend the affection of love, and afterward the works of charity.
57_marg507: As your rank of profession is more distinguished, so it is necessary that the care of virtue be more abundant, so that you embrace even those who do not love you with the bosom of charity.
57_marg508: There are two kinds of benefit: either when we give what we give out of goodwill, or when we lend to one who will return it.
57_interl582: or: they do good to you
57_interl583: solely because you hope to receive, not given for God
57_marg509: After he has refuted love and lending to sinners as unfruitful, now he shows how it ought to be done fruitfully by the faithful here. As if: although such love and lending do not profit sinners, yet you love, not only by the leading of nature, as they do friends, but by a higher degree of virtue, even enemies.
57_marg510: The philosophers divide justice into three parts: one toward God, which is called ‘piety’; another toward parents and the rest of the human race; a third toward the dead, so that funeral duties may be paid to them. But the Lord, surpassing the oracle of the law and the summit of philosophy, extended the office of piety even to those who have injured them.
57_marg511: Not fixing hope of reward on man. Whether he returns what you lent, God, at whose command you did it, will return it nonetheless; whether he does not return it, your inheritance will be forever.
57_interl587: “he gave them power to be made the sons of God”
57_marg513: Be ye therefore merciful, etc. It rains on the wicked, the earth does not deny its yield, and the same sun shines on good and bad. Mystically: he waters the Jewish people with prophetic rains, and the ray of the eternal sun shone on those who did not deserve it. If therefore they believe, be merciful to them by teaching and by lifting them up, and do not judge rashly, lest anyone conscious of his own guilt be compelled to pass sentence on another.
57_interl588: not only be merciful in the largess of benefits, but also in judging
57_marg514: There are some middle and uncertain things, as to the spirit in which they are done, because they can be done well or badly. We also do not know what the one who now appears wicked will be, and to despair of his correction and rebuke him as one cast off is rash.
57_marg515: Concerning open things which cannot be done with a good intention, we are permitted to judge.
57_marg516: A heaped measure (mensuram confersam): crammed, crammed more; hence more packed, packed together.
57_interl598: they will be the cause that God gives, because they were an occasion of merit
57_marg518: For with the same measure, etc. In general it can be taken of all, by whatever mind, hand or tongue the deeds are done, because God will repay according to the works of each.
57_marg519: Ambrose. God does not repay with an unjust measure. It is as if he said: the very rashness of judging and an unjust measure harm you and punish you, and often not him whom you are judging. Or if you judge rightly and it profits you by merit, it saves you; and if sometimes not him to whom you bestow these things.
57_marg520: He spoke also to them a likeness, etc. A likeness by which he invites them to give alms and to forgive injury.
57_interl599: a fool to teach a fool
57_marg521: If anger has blinded you against a violent man, if you are greedy against one who asks, can you cure his vice by your mind when it is itself corrupted? Not only will he who wronged you be guilty, but you too, who know not how to bear it. But if his wickedness finds you calm and he repents, you will be crowned for your patience, because you have taken care to lead the blind man to the light, that is, with a calm heart, by the eye that sees.
57_marg522: God does not avenge his own wrongs, but wished by enduring persecutors to make them milder. Disciples, who are men, ought to imitate this rule of perfection.
57_interl603: a lighter fault, or whatever disturbs the eye of the mind
57_marg523: Truly a sinner cannot rebuke a sinner, because those who are preoccupied with pride or hatred or some other vice, judging these light faults or none, sharply rebuke those whom they see disturbed in mind by anger or some slight sin. Such people prefer to vituperate and condemn rather than to correct and amend.
57_marg524: Thou considerest not, etc. An open eye sees badly, namely in boasting of itself while it wishes to heal another; but blind to itself, it cannot look at itself, while in this it falls worse.
57_interl606: you cannot correct anger in your brother, the lesser thing, until you have driven hatred or envy, the greater, out of your heart
57_interl607: for one who has not yet healed himself is not fit to heal another first, as a teacher
57_marg525: Hypocrite, etc. If you wish to rebuke anyone, first see whether you are like him. But if you are, groan together with him, and do not have him obey you, but advise him to strive along with you. But if you are not like him, yet because you once were, or could have been, stoop down and rebuke him, not out of hatred but out of mercy. Rarely, therefore, and only out of great necessity, are rebukes to be administered, and not unless, with regard to God, the beam has been removed from the eye.
57_marg526: For these take it upon themselves to accuse everything out of hatred or envy, and wish to seem counsellors without an example of their own amendment. But they ought first to remove the beam of envy or malice or pretence from the hidden place of their heart, so that they may be able to cast out the mote of anger, or of some fault of spite, from the eye of their brother.
57_marg527: For there is no good tree, etc. The good or bad tree is not nature, which God created good in all things, but the good or bad will. The fruits are works, which cannot be good of an ill will, nor evil of a good will.
57_marg528: If you wish to have true righteousness, and not feigned, fulfil with deeds what you show with words, so that you may be a good tree and adorned with good fruits. For even if a hypocrite pretends, he who does evil works is not good; and even if he rebukes an innocent man, he who does good works is not therefore evil. And note that what is treated here is what is manifest.
57_marg529: The wicked are known by their fruit, while they oppress the good; and if they do not blaspheme God in words, they do so in deeds, and most of all they are known by impatience in time of adversity. For fasts and prayer and the like are common to the feigned as to the good. But sheep ought not to lay aside their skins, even if sometimes wolves cover themselves with them.
57_marg530: They are known not by their clothing but by the works that are done by them, because as a thorn does not produce a grape, so a good tree produces good, a bad one bad, and not the reverse.
57_marg531: Not from thorns, that is, the cares of the world. Figs, that is, the sweetness of resurrection; nor from a bramble, that is, the stinging of vices. Grape, that is, the fruit of the soul, which, like a grape placed near earthly things, is spoiled, but in higher things ripens. Or: from the flesh, which produces thorns and thistles, we do not gather the grape, Christ, who hung on the tree like a cluster.
57_marg532: Thorn and bramble: heretics, from whom none of the wise can find holiness or virtue, but who tear and wound those who approach them. Or thorns and brambles: the cares of the world and the stings of vices. Grape and fig: the sweetness of a new way of life, which Christ hungers for in us, and ‘the fervour of love’ which gladdens the heart of man. Neither grape nor fig comes from thorns and brambles, because the mind of the old man, still pressed by old custom, can indeed feign, but cannot bear the fruit of the new man. But if at any time the deeds or words of the wicked profit the good, the wicked do not do this; it is done by the counsel of God concerning them.
57_marg533: He loves his enemy; he gives to everyone who asks, and the like. He brings forth evil, hates a friend, takes what belongs to others, does not give what is his own, and the like; these God judges according to the intention of the heart. And rightly so, because the fruit ought to be judged good or evil according as it proceeds from a good or evil heart: because out of the abundance of the heart, which lies hidden within, the mouth speaks, that is, the effect proceeds outwardly, both in words and in deeds. This is with regard to the divine examination, to which the mouth of the heart speaks, for he does not fail to know with what intention words proceed. He also judges that words which seem good outwardly are not good, since they proceed from a bad root. Whence he adds: “And why call you me, Lord, Lord?” as if to say: why do you boast that you put forth the leaves of right confession, when you show no fruits of good work?
57_interl616: the treasure of the heart is the same as the root of the tree; what is brought forth from the heart is the same as the fruit of the tree
57_marg534: Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks, etc. By the speech of the mouth the Lord signifies everything that is brought forth from the heart, in deed or in thought. For a word is also customarily put for a deed. Whence: “There was no word which he did not show them.”
57_interl618: to God, even if not to men
57_marg535: This calling seems to be the fruit of a good tree, but because it does not proceed from the richness of charity, God does not judge it good. But what the true discernment of good and bad fruits is, he sets forth under another figure: “Every one that cometh to me.”
57_marg536: Every one that cometh, etc. After he has long discoursed about the openly wicked, and about the truly good and the feigned good, he likens the good hearers of the word to himself, and the bad to the devil. For just as Christ builds, teaches and governs one Church through various persons, to lead it into eternal life, so the good hearer builds for himself, by various virtues, a heavenly dwelling, to rejoice in the future with Christ at its dedication. And just as the devil draws those obedient to him from heaven to earthly things and to sins, where there is no foundation, because evil is without substance and always hurls them into worse things, so the evil hearer, whether he be initiated in the mysteries of Christ or wholly a stranger to them, falls like one thrown into a well without a bottom, and finds nowhere to hold himself; but when he has come to the depth of evils, he scorns it.
57_interl622: the Church, in which he remains forever
57_marg537: He digs deep who, by the precepts of humility, utterly uproots all earthly things from the hearts of his own, so that he does not serve God for the sake of some fleeting thing, and so that God may have in them an unshaken dwelling.
57_marg538: Foundations: in the plural, teachers; in the singular, foundation: Christ, the teacher of teachers.
57_marg539: The foundations of the house are the intentions of a good way of life, which the perfect hearer lays within himself, once the rubble of superfluous thoughts has been cleared away by Christian humility, doing in himself spiritually what Christ does generally in the whole Church.
57_interl623: the rock was Christ, to whose faith and love the holy Church prefers nothing
57_marg540: Elsewhere he calls this flood “the gates of hell”: “and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” This flood happens in three ways: because each one is tempted by his own concupiscence, or by the wickedness of false brethren, or by the open assault of outsiders.
57_marg541: The flood: “The stream of the river maketh the city of God joyful: the most High hath sanctified his own tabernacle. God is in the midst thereof.” By the rush of the river can be understood the peril of the last judgment, when the Church is perfected in both; “Every one that exalteth himself shall be humbled, and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.”
57_marg542: Each of our houses is daily beaten by the restlessness either of unclean spirits or of wicked men, or of one’s own mind or flesh. And so far as they trust in their own strength, they are bent; but so far as they cling to the most unconquerable rock, they cannot be shaken.
57_interl628: “The stream of the river maketh the city of God joyful: the most High hath sanctified his own tabernacle. God is in the midst thereof, it shall not be moved.”
57_interl629: it can rush in, but not overthrow
57_interl630: because it stands, it is attributed not to itself but to God
57_interl631: what therefore falls is not built in Christ
57_interl632: outwardly, and therefore has no excuse
57_interl633: of whom it is said: an enemy man has done this
57_marg543: The devil builds “the world which is set in evil” upon the earth, because he draws it to love of earthly things; he builds without foundation, because sin does not subsist in its own nature, since evil is not a substance; which nevertheless, wherever it occurs in a good nature, takes hold; or “without foundation” means “without bottom.” Just as one who sinks into a well is held by the bottom of the well, so a fallen soul stands as if in some place at the bottom, if it holds itself within some measure of sin. But when it cannot remain content with the sin into which it slips, and is daily led to worse things, it does not find a bottom on which to fix itself, as in the well into which it has fallen.
57_marg544: Every conscience which does not remain fixed in hope in God cannot persist in temptations, and it is the more driven about the more it is cut off from higher things by those things which are of the world. And truly, all the wicked, or feigned good, become worse when any temptation besets them.
57_interl635: because he despised the warnings of salvation
57_marg545: Beautifully, once he has completed the precepts, he teaches the pattern for carrying out his precepts. For straightway the servant of the Gentile centurion is offered to the Lord to be healed, in whom the Gentiles, who were held sick in worldly servitude, are represented as to be saved by the benefit of God.
57_interl638: to which he had come down
57_interl639: from the summit of the mountain
57_marg546: He did not enter before he had finished his words, and yet he did not enter immediately after these words. For before he entered, in that very interval, the leper was cleansed, as Matthew relates.
57_interl640: unless he had been restored to life by the faith of the one who prayed to God and by the pity of Christ, who has mercy; in which it is noted that he so loved his enemies as to snatch them from death and give them the hope of eternal salvation
57_marg547: Mystically. The Gentile people, whose figure the centurion bears, does not hold Jesus far from his house, though he does not dare to have him come under his roof, because: “Surely his salvation is near to them that fear him.” He who rightly uses the natural law, so that he does the good things he knows, thereby draws near to him who is truly good. But for those whom the crimes of the error of the Gentiles had bound, what is said elsewhere can be applied: “For some of them came from afar.”
57_marg548: Although about to heal powerfully by a word alone, to commend humility he deigns to visit the sick man; and he who was unwilling to go to heal the petty king’s son, lest he should seem to have honoured riches, goes to the servant, lest he should be thought to have scorned a servile condition. Faith shines forth in works while he heals, but humility works more in affections while he goes.
57_marg549: By divine providence the elders of the Jews are sent, and with them present the sick man is healed, so that they may be inexcusable if they have refused to believe.
57_marg550: The centurion sends friends, lest his own presence should seem to burden the Lord’s modesty and to challenge office with office. But it signifies that we who believe from among the Gentiles cannot ourselves come to God, whom we cannot see in the flesh, but approach by faith him who sits at the right hand of the Father. The Gentile people, like the centurion, is surrounded by a soldiery of virtues and of spiritual perfection, which is signified by the hundred. Lofty, asking the Lord nothing earthly for himself or his own, but only the joys of eternal salvation. And these ask for their servants, that is, for those who are still pressed in fear by the spirit of servitude, beseeching the Lord that, as these are gradually advanced to higher things, “perfect charity may cast out fear.”
57_marg551: Matthew says that the centurion came to him, which is to be understood through faith. For it is truly through faith that one approaches God, which is commended by the Lord in the centurion: “I have not found so great faith in Israel.” Moreover, Luke follows the order in which the things were done, so that we may understand how Matthew says he came to him.
57_marg552: With the swagger of a soldier laid aside, he takes up reverence; easy to faith, prompt to honour.
57_marg553: Because of the conscience of a Gentile life, he thought himself burdened rather than helped by the Lord’s condescension, and that he could not have Christ as a guest; for though endowed with faith in him, he was not yet imbued with the sacraments. But because divine grace knows how to give what human weakness does not presume, in the figure of the Gentile people, he deserved that his faith, though not yet instructed by the Lord, be praised, and his servant healed.
57_interl641: great faith, which believes that for God to say is to do
57_marg554: For I also, etc. If I, a man under another, can command those beneath me, how much more can you, who have angels serving you over all things, by their ministry, without bodily presence, say to infirmity that it depart, and it will depart; and to health that it come, and it will come.
57_interl645: not as one of a troubled mind, but as teaching us, who need to be advised, to marvel at things of this kind
57_interl646: except among the apostles and in the blessed Mary
57_interl647: of the present time; for he found it among the ancients
57_marg555: Even in this one case, the faith of the Gentiles is preferred to Israel.
57_marg556: This man’s faith is preferred even to the more chosen ones who see God.
57_marg557: Matthew explains more plainly that, when the Lord said: “As you have believed, let it be done for you. Let the boy be healed.” But it is the custom of blessed Luke to shorten what others have set out in full. Or also to pass over on purpose, and more skilfully to make clear, what others have said briefly or left out.
57_marg558: The master believing, the servant is healed, because the merit of the master can also avail servants, not only by the merit of faith but also by the zeal of discipline.
57_marg559: And it came to pass, etc. After healing the sick man he raises the dead, because sickness precedes death.
57_marg560: Naim is a city of Galilee, at the second mile from Thabor towards the south, near Endor, which is a large village. Naim is interpreted as “waves” or “commotion.”
57_marg561: Bede. When “The Word was made flesh” was leading the Gentile people through the gates of faith into the heavenly Jerusalem, behold, the Jewish people, the lesser, dead through unbelief, is carried out; whom mother Church, possessing nothing in the world as her own, surrounded by many crowds of peoples, weeps for with holy affection and labours to call back to life with pious tears. This she obtains in the meantime in a few converted Jews, and at last in the fullness of them.
57_marg562: The dead man, who is carried out before many outside the gate, signifies one “sinning criminally,” who does not cover the sin in the bed of the heart, but reveals it to others by the evidence of work or speech, as through the doors of his city. Mother Church weeps for him as for an only son; she, though gathered from many persons, is nevertheless one, the virgin mother Church, and the individuals are her sons. The gate by which he is carried out is one of the senses by which someone falls into sin: as the one who looks to lust, the one who lends his ear to idle or shameful things, the one who lends his tongue to quarrels.
57_marg563: The only son of his mother. Ambrose. Adam is carried from the earth by the four elements, of which man consists. The bier is touched by God, that is, by the wood of the cross, because Adam perished through the wood of paradise. Man is carried by earth when he thinks only of earthly things, or when he is sick and cannot walk. He is carried by water when he thinks of luxury, or when, from excessive cold, the body cannot be touched. He is carried by air when he does everything for human praise, or when he cannot breathe because of sickness. He is carried by fire when he thinks of avarice, or when, from excessive fever, he cannot be touched.
57_interl650: The widow is the Church, which, redeemed by the death of her spouse, is a pilgrim, away from him, for the time of her sojourning.
57_marg564: Many with the Lord, many with the widow, so that, the miracle having been seen, many may become praisers and witnesses of God.
57_interl651: Bede. He is first moved by mercy: behold an example of pity to be imitated. Afterwards he raises him, in which the faith in his wondrous power is established.
57_interl652: the dead man whom you will soon see rise again
57_marg565: The bier on which he is carried out is the careless conscience of the despairing sinner, which bears him to be buried; either unclean desires or the flatteries of those who praise him, which, like a heap of earth, bury the sinners. But when the Lord touches the sinner’s conscience, the crowd of carnal pleasures and unjust praises is restrained by fear of the coming judgment, and the mind, returned to itself, runs to life to meet God calling it, and answers by obeying the Saviour.
57_marg566: The bier on which the body is carried is the human body. The bearers are evil habits, which drag the body itself to death. But Jesus touches the bier when he raises our frail nature on the wood of the cross. Then the bearers of the funeral stand still, because they can no longer drag to death as before; then Jesus speaks, that is, he pours in the warnings of salvation. At this word, heard, the sick man is raised to life and speaks of him in good deeds, and so is given back to his mother, that is, the Church.
57_marg567: And Bede. And he that was dead, sat up, etc. The Lord raised three dead: the ruler’s daughter in the house, that is, in thought; the only son of the mother at the gate, that is, in word; Lazarus in the tomb, that is, in deed.
57_interl654: showing a return to life for those who had bewailed their sin
57_interl655: joined to the communion of the Church by priestly judgment
57_interl656: the more desperate the death of the soul which is recalled to life, the more many are corrected by the same, and the greater the Lord’s mercy is understood to be
57_marg568: While he both decided that the Word should be made flesh once, and daily sends the Holy Ghost into the hearts of men, that they may be raised up.
57_marg569: Ambrose. Not with a simple heart, but with envy goading him. 57_marg570: But because envy could not yet be driven out, he sends them to Jesus, so that on this occasion they may see the signs, and, corrected, believe in Jesus, and, the master asking, may say to him: “Art thou he that art to come?”
57_marg571: Allegorically. John is a figure of the Law, which, foretelling Christ, was held shut up in the breasts of the faithless as in prisons emptied of light, so that it could not put forth the full testimony of the Lord’s dispensation without the witness of the Gospel. He therefore sends the disciples to Christ, so that they may attain the completion of knowledge, because Christ is the fulfilment of the Law; so that, since words without deeds often wavered, faith might be shown fuller by the testimony of deeds than by the promises of words, and what then wavered in the breasts of the Jews, as the Law was obscured, might be laid open by that very spectacle of the Lord’s cross and by the full testimony of the resurrection. For the Law foretells doubtfully that Christ is to come; the Gospel, where so many miracles are shown, most certainly confirms that he has come.
57_marg572: Gregory. He does not say, “you who have come,” as if to say: when I am to be slain by Herod and about to descend to the underworld, ought I to announce to the dead him whom I announced to the living? Or is it fitting for the Son of God to die, or are you going to send another to these mysteries? For a pious prophet, who had foretold that he was to come, could not have believed that he was going to die; he doubted, not from lack of faith but from piety, because a slip of love does not impair faith. For such a slip is a religious one.
57_marg573: Jesus, knowing that no one can fully believe without the gospel, because just as faith begins with the Old Testament, so it is fulfilled in the New, when asked about himself, marked himself out not by any word but by deeds; not answering the things that were asked, but for the stumbling of the messengers.
57_marg574: Behold the full testimony that he is the Son of God. For before the gospel these were either rare or none. Whence Tobias recovered his sight, and this was the medicine of an angel, not of a man. Elias raised the dead, yet himself prayed and wept. Eliseus caused a leper to be cleansed, yet there the authority of the command did not avail, but the figure of a mystery. But since these are still small examples of the Lord’s testimony, he adds, after the things said above, about the cross and death and burial, which is the fullness of faith. For there is no greater testimony of the divine person than to have offered himself whole, as one, for the world; by this alone is the Lord fully declared, as he was also declared by John: “Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sin of the world.”

57_marg575: Blessed is he, etc. As if to say: indeed I do wonders, but I do not disdain to suffer abject things; and men must take care lest those who venerate the signs despise in me the death.
57_marg576: Gregory. He who has not doubted of the power of the divinity. This is not said against John, whom he at once commends so highly, but he calls back the unbelieving from unbelief, and explains to John what he was asking, since: “Our God is the God of salvation: and of the Lord, of the Lord are the issues from death.” Having seen so many signs and virtues, the faithful man could not doubt his death, but could only marvel; but the mind of the unbelievers endured scandal in him, since they saw him dying even after the miracles.
57_marg577: lest the crowds suspect that John was moved by envy, and that they may know he asked not for himself but for his disciples.

57_marg578: What went ye out into the desert to see? etc. Where he admonished John’s disciples that they must believe in the Lord’s cross, turned to the crowds, he challenges the poor to virtue, lest, exalted in heart, unstable in mind, weak in counsel, they prefer showy things to useful ones and fleeting things to eternal ones, but rather take up the cross than the trappings of the world. And therefore he praises the person of John, who, having set love of life behind him, did not change the form of justice for fear of death. The world is compared to a desert, because it is still uncultivated and barren, into which one must not go forth in such a way that we think men puffed up in the mind of the flesh, empty of virtue, and boasting of the glory of the fragile world, are to be imitated.
57_marg579: A reed. Bede. By the reed is signified the carnal mind, which, touched by favour or by detraction, is bent to whichever side. But John is not a reed shaken by the wind, because neither favour made him soft, nor did anyone’s anger make him harsh; prosperity did not raise him up, nor adversity bend him.
57_interl661: who is driven by every wind, so that by lightness of mind he doubts concerning me, whom he preached
57_marg580: What went you out to see? How could they desire to see John in the desert, who was shut up in prison? So this whole discourse must be understood spiritually.
57_marg581: Led by vainglory, he seeks profit for feasts or clothes, he who lives on locusts and is clothed in camel’s hair.
57_marg582: By the garment the human body is understood. Therefore, by a prophetic example, he exhorts to take up virtue: “Behold they that are in costly apparel.” By whose riches the limbs are loosened, the strangers to the heavenly kingdom grow old within the dwellings of this world under the rule of the devils, who are the kings of darkness.
57_marg583: Allegorically: John was not clothed in soft things, who did not cherish the life of sinners with flatteries, but rebuked them harshly.
57_marg584: Note: a rigid life and preaching ought to shun the palaces of the soft, which the soft-clad flatterers frequent. Let no one think that sin is lacking in fickleness and devotion to clothes; otherwise he would not have been praised for the roughness of his garments.
57_marg585: It is the office of a prophet to foretell what is to come, not also to show it. The greater prophet is one in whom is the end of the prophets.
57_interl662: who place cushions under the elbow; who flatter, not prick, the life of sinners
57_marg586: who foretold that I was to come, and also pointed me out with his finger.
57_marg587: And more than a prophet, etc. Because he is an angel not by nature but by office, who is sent to announce the heavenly Judge.
57_marg588: by the way, he renders to you the hearts of the hearers, preaching penance and baptizing.

57_marg589: In this he is not preferred to the patriarchs and to all men, but is shown to be equal to the other saints.

57_marg590: Every saint who is already with God is greater than one who is still in the world. Or: I, whom the opinion of many makes lesser, am preferred to him in the Church of the saints. Or: the lowest angel of heaven is better than any man.
57_marg591: If this is understood as said by the Lord, then by “hearing John” the peoples are understood to be designated; if it is said to be inserted by the evangelist, it remains to be understood as the people hearing the Lord himself discoursing about John’s greatness.
57_marg592: God is justified through baptism, while men justify themselves by confessing their own sins, as it is written: “You, tell your iniquities, that you may be justified.” And he is justified in him who is not refuted through obstinacy, but whose gift is recognized through the justice of God: “For the Lord is just, and has loved righteous deeds.” In him, then, is God’s justification, if he appears to have conferred his gifts not on the unworthy and harmful, but on the innocent made clean by washing, even on the just. He therefore who confesses sin to God justifies God, yielding to him who conquers, and hoping for grace from him. In baptism, therefore, God is justified, in which there is confession and forgiveness of sins.

57_marg594: Whereunto then, etc. Having praised John, he passes to rebuke those who were not moved by John’s preaching, and who despise the preaching of Christ himself.
57_marg595: Children are teachers, humble in spirit. The marketplace, “the synagogue” or “Jerusalem itself,” in which the laws of God’s precepts were laid down, because they used to reproach their fellow citizens that they, though enticed by the psalms, did not rise to the praises of God with devoted heart, nor with agility of limbs, which the leaping denotes; nor, by the Lamentations, that is, the laments of the prophets over the ruins already made or yet to be made, were they turned to penance.
57_interl678: where law and rights are proclaimed
57_marg596: as: “Be converted to me with all your heart, in fasting, and in weeping,” and the like; but “My people is foolish; they have not known me.”
57_marg597: We have piped, etc. A wedding song, in which the soul marries the Word, the flesh the Spirit. In these nuptials David wanted us to play, saying: “Rejoice to God our helper; sing aloud to the God of Jacob; take a psalm, and bring hither the timbrel.” As if to say: the prophet, placed in the very act of the wedding, leaps with a certain joy; but “my people heard not my voice: and Israel hearkened not to me.”
57_marg598: by the example of his abstinence, declaring penance to you, and you were unwilling to be humbled with him.
57_marg599: by food and drink foreshowing the joy of the age to come, and you were unwilling to rejoice with him, but you slandered him.
57_marg600: The Son of man is come, etc. He came as then, so now too, you reject both ways of salvation. We mourned to John; we sang to Christ.
57_marg601: He shows that the children of wisdom understand that righteousness lies not in abstaining, nor in eating, but in bearing want with equanimity and in temperance, not corrupting oneself by abundance: “The kingdom of God is not meat and drink.” It is not their use, but the desire for them, that is rebuked.
57_marg602: Justified, etc. Whatever you may think of me, I nevertheless am understood, by the apostles, to whom the Father revealed what he hid from the prudent, to act justly as the power of God and the wisdom of God.
57_interl680: that is, by the just, and afterwards by those who repent into justice
57_marg603: Desired him. As he had proposed in words, so also in deeds he establishes that wisdom is justified by all her children, since also by Mary, who repented after her fault.
57_marg604: Mystically. The Pharisee, presuming on false righteousness, signifies the Jewish people, who invite the Lord to a feast, because whom they did not believe coming, they do not cease to hope will come. But still with a vow they say: “Stir up thy might, and come.” The house of the Pharisee is “the law and the prophets,” in which that people gloried to have their dwelling. This house, appearing in the flesh, he enters, because “he came not to destroy the law but to fulfil it.” “He reclined,” because in his majesty he was not understood; he became visible in the form of a servant. But the Gentiles, given over to unclean acts, come to know through the report of the apostolic preaching that “God sent his Son, made in the flesh, made under the law.” Not that the Pharisee, who attends only to the letter, is justified; but the house, that is, we who follow the grace of the Spirit in the law, who do not blame that he receives sinners, but praise that he justifies sinners.
57_marg605: In the house of the Pharisee the sinner merits grace, because the knowledge of sin comes through the law; thus the law sends her to grace in the house of the Pharisee.
57_marg606: Into whatever inner house you find wisdom and justice reclining, run to the feet, that is, to the furthest part of wisdom; seek with tears, confess sins, spread your hair, that is, lay before him all the dignities of your body; kiss, that is, speak nothing but wisdom.
57_interl682: she sets out to snatch the grace of the host
57_marg607: As many delights as she had in herself, so many burnt offerings she found of herself.
57_interl683: a kind of marble in which unguents are kept uncorrupted
57_marg608: She brings ointment because she does good works, by which she sprinkles the Church with the fragrance of a good reputation. Whence it is said: “We are the good odour of Christ unto God” in every place.
57_marg609: The alabaster box of ointment: that is, the body with faith. Standing behind: that is, after the ascension of the Lord. By the feet: that is, the apostles. Wet with tears: that is, with inner love in God. Wiped with the hairs: that is, she gives away superfluous food and clothing. She kisses: she has peace with everyone. One owed five hundred pence: these are the sins of the Gentiles, committed by the five senses. The other, fifty: that is, the sins of the Jews.
57_marg610: Standing against the feet is he who, placed in sins, resists the Lord’s ways. But he who is turned to penance after sins now stands behind, by the feet, while he follows the footsteps of the Lord that he was attacking. He waters the feet with tears who suffers with the tribulations of the saints, who thinks their sadness his own, who bows down to the last members of Christ by the affection of compassion. With the hairs, which are superfluous to the body, he wipes the feet he had watered: he who begins to have mercy, from earthly substance which is superfluous, on the saints to whom out of charity he sympathises. He kisses the feet who diligently loves those to whom he gives his goods, lest the necessity of the neighbour be burdensome to the giver. He anoints with ointment who, by doing good works, sprinkles others with the fragrance of a good reputation, and by his example leads them to do good. Or, through the feet can be signified the flesh of Christ, which we kiss while we love the mystery of his Incarnation. We anoint, while by good report we proclaim the power of his humanity in holy speech. But the Pharisee, seeing this, is envious, because when the Jews see the Gentiles preach God, they waste away in their malice; to them the Lord enumerates the good things of the Gentiles, so that they may know in what evils they themselves lie.
57_interl684: weeping, now by penance breaking the eyes with which she had craved earthly things
57_marg611: Mary, sister of Lazarus, performed the same office twice: once in Galilee, when she first came with humility and tears, where she received the forgiveness of sins; a second time in Bethania, no longer named a sinner but chaste, and therefore devout: there she anoints the feet, here the head.
57_marg612: So also the faithful soul, first humbled at the feet of the Lord to be loosed from sins, is bent low; afterwards, as its merits grow, it pours the fragrance of joyful faith, like a perfume of spices, over the head of the Lord. So also the universal Church, in the present, celebrating the mysteries of the Incarnation of Christ, which is signified by the name of feet, renders devoted service to the Redeemer. In the future also, beholding together his glory as man and the eternity of his divinity (because the head of Christ is God), she will glorify him with perpetual songs of confession, as with pistic nard.
57_interl685: which she had shown for the arranging of her face.
57_interl687: with the mouth with which she had spoken proudly.

57_marg614: proud of false righteousness, moved by no compassion for human nature, forgetful of his own frailty.
