From this dust the feet of the evangelists are bidden to be washed by good hearers, and by the Saviour himself they are said to have been washed. But he who scorns the teaching of the preacher turns the labours and dangers and weariness of the anxieties to his own testimony of damnation. Hence this dust is bidden to be wiped off on the despisers of the gospel.
57_marg808: The Sodomites, though they burned with vices and were inhospitable, nevertheless among them no such guests were found as the prophets among the Jews, or the apostles. Lot among them, though just, nevertheless taught nothing and did no signs. And therefore: “To whom much is given, of him much shall be required”; and: “The mighty shall be mightily tormented.”
57_marg809: Corozain, Bethsaida, Capharnaum and Tiberias are cities of Galilee on the shore of the lake of Genesareth. The Lord laments these, because after so many miracles and mighty works they did not repent, and are worse than the Gentiles, who violate only the natural law; for after contempt of the written law they did not fear to trample underfoot the Son of God and to spurn grace in their ingratitude.
57_marg810: By sackcloth is signified the bitter memory of pricking sin, by which the left side must be clothed on the day of judgment. In ashes the consideration of death is figured, by which the whole mass of the human race is to be reduced to dust; in sitting, the humility of one’s own conscience. Whence the prophet: “Rise after you have sat”; that is: “Be you humbled under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in the time of visitation.”
57_marg811: We see the words of the Saviour fulfilled, since those aforesaid cities were unwilling to believe while the Lord was present. Tyre and Sidon were once friends of David and Solomon, and afterwards, when Christ’s disciples preached, they devoutly received the faith. Why it was preached to those who would not believe, and not preached to those who would believe, he knows who knows all things.
57_marg812: And thou, Capharnaum, etc. Either you are exalted, proudly resisting my preaching; or you have been exalted by my hospitality and my signs and powers, and therefore you will be punished with a greater punishment, because you were unwilling to believe in these things. And lest anyone think these words apply only to those cities or persons who did not receive the Lord in the flesh, he adds: “He that heareth you, heareth me.” In hearing or despising the preacher of the gospel, let each one know that it is not base persons but the Saviour himself whom he hears or despises, since in the disciple the master is heard, and in the Son the Father is honoured.
57_interl805: not showing mercy to one of the least of my brethren, has not shown it to me
57_interl806: unwilling to believe in the Son of God
57_interl807: because: “I and the Father are one.”
57_interl808: which was not in the law
57_marg813: They confess well, bearing honour to the name of Christ; but because they are still weak in faith, they rejoice in the powers and are elated by the working of signs; they are terrified by the example and called back to humility. For if the devil was cast down from heaven on account of pride, much more will these, made from the earth, be humbled if they have grown proud.
57_interl809: then, when he fell, I was present
57_interl810: thus fallen headlong from the heights to the depths
57_interl811: or as lightning, because, though cast down, he still “transformeth himself into an angel of light”
57_interl812: who wound openly with the tooth
57_marg814: Upon serpents. The serpents are evil men or devils, who cast the poisons of perverse persuasion against virtues just beginning. The scorpions are those who strive to spoil virtues that are to be perfected at the end.
57_interl813: who lie in wait secretly with the tail
57_marg815: You are able to cast out all unclean spirits from possessed bodies. Or literally: as the viper did not harm Paul’s hand, and the draught of poison did not harm John. Whence the Lord himself: “And if they shall drink any deadly thing, it shall not hurt them.”
57_marg816: To cast out evil spirits and to work other powers is sometimes not the merit of the one who works them; rather the invocation of Christ’s name does this, either for the condemnation of those who invoke, or for the benefit of those who see and hear, where, although men despise those who work signs, they nevertheless honour God, at whose invocation miracles happen. He forbids rejoicing at the humbling of the devil, who fell through pride; let them rejoice rather in their own exaltation, so that these, being humbled, may rise to where those fell from when they were lifted up.
57_interl814: which are held cheap by the world
57_marg817: If anyone has done works, whether heavenly or earthly, through these, because he is recorded in the writings, he is eternally fixed in God’s memory.
57_interl815: through the humility of your faith
57_interl816: concerning the salvation of the humble to whom he was speaking
57_marg818: When he was speaking of the subjection of unclean spirits and of names written in heaven, he showed through what the great loftiness was given to men, namely through the humility of Christian faith.
57_marg819: I confess. I give thanks, because at my coming you have revealed the mysteries to the apostles, which the scribes and Pharisees, who seem wise to themselves, do not know.
57_interl819: who do not know how to exalt themselves
57_marg820: He does not say to the foolish and dull, but to little ones, that is, the humble, so that he proves that he has condemned swelling pride, not keenness of mind.
57_interl820: what has pleased the just one cannot be unjust
57_marg821: He does not give the reason why he chose these and rejected those, but says that it was so pleasing to God. In this we take an example of humility, that we not rashly examine the heavenly counsels.
57_marg822: All things, etc. Humility having been commended, through which one comes to faith, the passage is beautifully joined to faith itself, when he says that all things are delivered to him: not the elements which he himself created, but those little ones to whom the Father revealed the mysteries of the Son.
57_marg823: When you hear “all things,” you acknowledge the Almighty, not one unlike or degenerate from the Father. When you hear “delivered,” you confess the Son, to whom all things are his own by right, by the nature of the one substance, not conferred as a gift by grace.
57_interl821: the inner eyes, not the outward eyes of the Pharisees, who saw my body
57_interl822: recognize those mysteries that are revealed to the little ones
57_interl823: to whom I have revealed myself and the Father
57_marg824: The prophets and just men saw the glory of the Lord from afar, “through a glass in a dark manner”; but the apostles, having the Lord present and asking him what they wished, were taught not through angels or various kinds of visions.
57_interl826: holding the words of the law, ignorant of the force of the law
57_marg825: The teacher of the law, who lay in the law without faith, rises that he may stand. He stands while he calls him master, but by standing he also tempts God, by keeping silent about what he really was.
57_marg826: The lawyer takes the occasion of tempting from the Lord’s words where he says: “Rejoice in this, that your names are written in heaven.” But in his temptation he shows how true was the Lord’s confession, by which, praising the Father, he says: “Thou hast hid these things from the wise and mighty, and hast revealed them to little ones.”
57_interl827: he asks what is written, so that by his own answers he may be justified or condemned
57_marg827: He said what he had read, but did not fulfil what was written, because he had before him the Lord whom he ought to love; yet he calls this one master, not God.
57_marg828: He shows the perfect way of heavenly life, while he answers the lawyer, who set forth what was written about the love of God and of neighbour: “Thou hast answered right: this do, and thou shalt live.” And when the parable was finished he added: “Go, and do thou in like manner.” In this he shows that by love alone one comes to eternal life. But that man had no neighbour, since he had perhaps never shown mercy, and therefore did not know one.
57_interl828: he praises the answer; he does not praise the deed
57_marg829: This do, and thou shalt live, etc. From the first chapter of the law he teaches the one ignorant of the law, proving that the law at the beginning straightway proclaimed the Father and the Son and announced the incarnation of the Son, saying: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God, and thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.” Whence he also adds: “This do, and thou shalt live.” But he, since he did not know his neighbour because he did not believe in Christ, answered: “And who is my neighbour?” So he who does not know Christ does not know the law either. For how can he know the law, when he is ignorant of the truth, since the law proclaims the truth?
57_interl829: because he thought he stood not before God but before a man, and he does not recognize as his neighbour the one whom he calls master
57_marg830: So that he may be said to have answered wisely, the lawyer first confesses that he is ignorant of the commandment of the law, because, refusing to be humbled and wishing to justify himself, he cannot see the hidden things that are revealed to the little ones of Christ. To him Christ so tempers the answer that everyone who shows mercy is understood to be a neighbour, and especially the Son of God himself, who by his humanity became our neighbour, is pointed out.
57_marg831: And who is my neighbour, etc. No one is nearer to man than God, who knows inwardly and outwardly and can care for all things; but every unbeliever or tempter has neither God nor man as a neighbour.
57_marg832: The priest of God announces the law: indeed the law came down into the world through Moses and conferred no health on man. The Levite came down, who shows the type of the prophets; but he too heals no one, because the law convicts of sins but passes by, since it does not grant pardon.
57_marg833: This was not said of the priest and the Levite, because the law has no mercy, but judgment and vengeance.
57_marg834: A certain man, etc. This man is understood to be Adam in the human race, who through the falling of transgression came down from the blessedness of the heavenly Jerusalem to the miseries and failings of this changeable and erring life, when he began to swell with pride. And through this he also fell among robbers, that is into the power of the angels of night, who transform themselves into angels of light but cannot persevere. He would not have fallen among them unless he had made himself liable again by disobeying the commandment of heaven. They also strip away the garments of spiritual grace, namely immortality and innocence, and so inflict wounds, that is sins, by which the integrity of human nature is violated, and death is brought in as though into the pits of the bowels. He who keeps unharmed the garments he has received cannot feel the blows of the robbers. They went away, not ceasing from ambushes, but concealing their ambushes. Leaving him half-alive, because they were able to strip off immortality but cannot abolish the sense of reason, so that man may still be wise and know God. The priest and the Levite, who pass by, figure the priesthood and ministry of the Old Testament, where the wounds of the languishing world are shown but not healed. The Samaritan, who is interpreted ‘keeper’, is the Lord, who, made man for our sake, undertook the journey of the present life and came near the wounded man: “In the likeness of men, and in habit found as a man.” He became our neighbour by taking up our compassion, and near by bestowing mercy. He bound up his wounds, restraining sins by rebuking them. He pours in oil while he gives hope to penitents, saying: “Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” He pours in wine while the Lord strikes into sinners the terror of punishment, saying: “Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit, shall be cut down, and shall be cast into the fire.” The beast is his flesh, in which he came to us, and on which he places the wounded man, because he bore our sins in his body. He is placed on it, indeed, who believes that very incarnation. The inn is the Church of the present time, where travellers returning to the eternal homeland are refreshed. Placed on the beast, he is led into the inn, because no one enters the Church except one who is baptized and joined to the body of Christ. And he took care of him, so that the sick man would not abandon the precepts he had received. But the Samaritan has no leisure to stay long on earth; he had to return to where he had come down from. So on the next day, that is, after his resurrection, when a fuller splendour of eternal light shone in the world than before the passion, he brought forth two pence, the two Testaments, in which the name and image of the eternal King are contained, and gave them to the innkeeper, that is, to the apostles, because then “he opened their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures,” for the governing of the people. Whatever thou shalt spend over and above. The apostle does more than is required when he says: “Now concerning virgins, I have no commandment of the Lord: but I give counsel.” He does more when he does not use the power of receiving necessities. Returning in judgment he will repay, saying: “Because thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will place thee over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.” Which of these? According to the letter it is plain that the foreigner was nearer to the man of Jerusalem, to whom he showed mercy, than the priest or the Levite of the same nation.
57_interl831: the chrism of the Holy Ghost
57_marg835: He brought him to an inn. He calls it not a house but an inn, a name by which he signifies the miseries and stench of this life, so that man should not rejoice in this exile as if in his homeland.
57_marg836: Kinship does not make a neighbour, but mercy, which is according to nature. For nothing is so according to nature as to help a fellow of one’s nature.
57_marg837: Allegorically. No one is nearer than he who has cured our wounds, who is one head with the members. Let us therefore love him as God and Lord. Let us love him as a neighbour; let us love also him who is an imitator of Christ. Whence follows: “Do thou in like manner,” that is, that you truly show yourself to love your neighbour as yourself, and whatever you are able to do, devotedly work for the relief of his bodily or spiritual need.
57_marg838: Having spoken of the love of God and of neighbour, an example of each love is set forth, not so much in word alone as in the performance of the work. For by these two sisters two spiritual lives are signified. By Martha, the devotion of active works, by which we are joined to our neighbour in charity. By Mary, the religious intention of the mind in the word of God, by which we sigh in the love of God. The active life gives bread to the hungry, or teaching to the ignorant; it corrects the one who errs, calls the proud back to humility, and dispenses what is useful to each. The contemplative life keeps the love of God and of neighbour, but rests from outward action, clings to the desire of the Creator alone, and, all cares trodden under foot, burns to see the face of the Creator and desires to be mingled with the heavenly citizens who rejoice in the eternal incorruption in the sight of the Lord.
57_marg839: Into her house, etc. When Jesus enters the house, a wicked life, even if it had once been there, flees away.
57_marg840: The lower one sits, the more one receives. Water flows together into a valley from the swellings of a hill.
57_marg841: Mary sits, because the contemplative, with the turmoil of vices calmed, now enjoys the desired peace of mind in Christ. Martha stands, because the active life, labouring, sweats in the struggle.
57_interl834: ministering the necessities to the mortal flesh in which the Son of God was clothed
57_marg842: Mary was intent on how she might be fed by the Lord; Martha was intent on how she might feed the Lord. Martha prepares a feast for the Lord; Mary already rejoices in the Lord’s banquet.
57_marg844: She speaks in the person of those who, still ignorant of divine contemplation, say that only the work of brotherly love which they have learned is pleasing to God, and therefore think that all who wish to be devoted to Christ must be given over to this.
57_marg845: Mary does not answer, but commits her cause to the judge, as one at leisure. For if she were preparing a reply, she would relax her attention to hearing.
57_marg846: The repetition is a sign of love, or perhaps of a purpose to admonish, so that she would listen more attentively.
57_marg847: that is, the best part which she chose
57_marg848: But one thing is necessary, etc. One thing is put before many. For it is not that one comes from many, but many from one; and yet many things are necessary for those who strive toward the one.
57_interl836: he who had been appealed to as judge became Mary’s advocate
57_marg849: Mary hath chosen the best part, etc. The part of Martha is not blamed, because it too is good; but the part of Mary is praised, and the reason why it is best is added: which shall not be taken away from her. For the contemplative life begins here and will be perfected in the heavenly homeland, since the fire of love, which begins to burn here, when it sees him whom it loves, will burn more brightly in love. The contemplative life therefore is not taken away; it is perfected when the light of this present age is withdrawn. The active life fails with the body, because in the eternal homeland it does not offer bread to the hungry, since no one will hunger, nor will it perform the other works of piety, since they will not be necessary. So the active life will be taken away with the present age. Rightly, therefore, the immense merits of justifications and the zealous practice of virtues are placed after contemplation.
57_marg850: Which shall not be taken away from her, etc. Understand by the opposite that from Martha will be taken away the part which she chose, because the labour of the multitude passes away, but the charity of unity remains.
57_marg851: After the history of the sisters, which signify two lives, he introduces the Lord praying and instructing the disciples to pray, because the prayer he taught also contains within itself the mystery of both lives, and the perfection of those lives is to be obtained not by our own strength but by prayers.
57_marg852: When he ceased, etc. Therefore the Saviour is often introduced praying, so that he may lead the disciples to the zeal of prayer. Hence, when the prayer is finished, he is asked by the disciples to teach them how they ought to pray.
57_marg853: When you pray, say, etc. Matthew sets down seven petitions: in three the eternal things are asked for, in four the temporal things, which nevertheless are necessary for attaining the eternal. For what we say: “Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven,” is begun here; however much we advance, these things grow in us and will be possessed perfectly without end in the other life. But what we say: “Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation. But deliver us from evil,” pertains to the need of the present life, because here both bread, bodily as well as spiritual, is necessary both to soul and to body. Here also the remission of the sins that are committed is made. Here temptations happen; here also happens the evil from which we desire to be freed. In the other life none of these is. Luke sets down not seven but five, and this for brevity. In the five that he sets down he understands those seven to be contained. For the name of God is sanctified in the spirit, and the kingdom of God is to come at the resurrection of the flesh. Luke, showing that the third petition is in a way a repetition of the two above, made it understood more by omitting it. Then he adds the three: concerning daily bread, concerning the remission of sins, concerning the temptation to be avoided. But as for what Matthew put last, “But deliver us from evil,” this one did not put, so that we would understand that it pertains to what was said about temptation. For Matthew does not say, “And deliver us from evil,” as though he set down a different petition; but he says, “But deliver us from evil,” showing it to be one petition, so that each may know that he is delivered from evil in that he is not led into temptation.
57_marg854: Daily bread is so called, which here is necessary, as much as is to be given to soul and flesh, whether it is understood bodily, spiritually, or in both ways.
57_marg855: Note that the lawyer, wishing to justify himself, approached to tempt the Lord, but went away confounded. But Mary, inclining at the feet, chose the best part of heavenly philosophy. Likewise the little ones of Christ, presuming not on their own righteousness but on the glory of the Redeemer, ask by what modes of prayer they ought to call upon the same grace, and they learn with what words to pray, and with what persistence to persevere, and for what things especially they ought to beseech, namely with faith, hope and charity; and that, asking perfectly, they receive from the Father the good Spirit, the giver of these same things. On the contrary, as is read in the lesson about the demoniac, the wise and prudent, who strive not to ask, seek and knock for the Spirit of grace, but to blaspheme, pay penalties that are irremissible both here and in the future for their obstinacy.
57_marg856: After he set forth the form of prayer for those who asked, he enjoins on them also urgency and frequency in praying, so that prayer is carried on not only by day but also by night; for he who asks bread of a friend at midnight, and persists in the purpose of asking, is not cheated, the one who prays.
57_marg857: The friend to whom one comes by night is God, who gave his body for us. To him in the night of tribulation we ought to pray, and to ask for three loaves, that is, the understanding of the holy Trinity, by which we may live in the labours of the present life. If you love the Lord thy God, you will be able to earn these loaves not only for yourself but also for others. The friend who comes from the road is our own soul, which, as often as it wanders off to seek temporal things, so often withdraws from us. It returns when it meditates on heavenly things and desires to be refreshed with heavenly nourishment. He has nothing to set before him, because the soul, sighing after God out of darkness, is pleased to think or say or look upon nothing except him, but only to gaze more at the joy of the Trinity which it has recognized, and to labour to attain to this.
57_interl839: I ought not to be disturbed by your prayers, because
57_marg858: It does not take away the hope of obtaining, but more vehemently kindles the desire of praying, the difficulty of attaining having been shown.
57_marg859: The door which Paul asked to be opened for him, to speak the mystery of Christ, and which John saw opened for himself, is the understanding of the divine word, which is closed in a time of famine of the word of God, when understanding is not given. And the children, that is, those who preached the wisdom of the gospel throughout the world, dispensing it like bread, are now with the Lord in eternal rest; and yet by praying it comes about that the one praying receives understanding from the Lord himself, even if no man is present through whom wisdom may be preached.
57_marg860: Ambrose. No one fears lest he rouse the sleeping one whom he knows to be always awake in prayer.
57_interl840: not frightened by shame but compelled by necessity
57_interl841: either by inspiring him himself or by sending a teacher
57_marg861: There are many snares, and the heavy sleep of the body; for if the mind begins to sleep, it loses the vigour of its virtue. Rouse therefore your sleep, that you may knock at the door of Christ, so that when you have entered, the hidden and dark treasures in Christ Jesus may be opened to you.
57_interl842: although not as much as he at some time wished
57_marg862: If a friend rises and gives, not from friendship but compelled by weariness, how much more does God give, who without weariness most abundantly bestows what is asked. Therefore, lest the soul, turned from the vanity of error, waste away longer in spiritual want, let us seek the feasts of the word; let us seek a friend who gives; let us knock at the door where hidden things are kept. For he who does not deceive in promising gives great hope. For everyone who asks, receives. Perseverance is needed that we may obtain. But if to him who asks it is given, and he who seeks finds, and to him who knocks it is opened, then to whom is it not given, and who does not find, and to whom is it not opened? It is plain that he has not sought, asked and knocked well.
57_marg863: Seek, and you shall find. “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth, and he will do the will of those who fear him.” James rebukes those who do not ask in this way, saying: “You ask, and receive not; because you ask amiss,” because you persist in sins.
57_marg864: We receive four things from the Lord. First, we receive the discipline of correction, by which we are amended. Proverbs 8: “O ye men, to you I call, and my voice is to the sons of men.” Second, the teaching of instruction, by which we are enlightened. John 17: “Because the words which thou gavest me, I have given to them; and they have received them, and have known in very deed that I came out from thee.” Third, the grace of love. First to the Corinthians, chapter 8: “I have not received.” Fourth, the glory of reward, through which we are strengthened, and this is most precious to us; and four things are necessary for obtaining it. First, the brightness of chastity. Second, the vigour of patience, as is seen in soldiers in tournaments: when they have fought well, they are crowned. James 1: “Blessed is the man that endureth temptation.” Third, the labour of penance. First to the Corinthians, chapter 13: “Every man shall receive his own reward.” Fourth, the love of voluntary poverty. Matthew 19, at the end: “Everyone who has left,” etc.
57_marg865: Bede. Mystically. Bread signifies charity, on account of its greater desirability and necessary use; for just as a table seems poor without bread, so without charity the other virtues are nothing, since they are perfected in charity alone. The hardness of heart contrary to this he compared to a stone. A fish is faith in things unseen. For just as the fish is born, lives and is fed under the covering of the waters, so faith which is in God is begotten invisibly in the heart, is consecrated invisibly through the water of baptism by the invisible grace of the Spirit, is nourished by the invisible help of divine protection lest it fail, and, looking to invisible rewards, does whatever good it can. Or else faith is likened to a fish for this reason: just as the fish is beaten by the frequent waves of the sea and yet is not destroyed, so faith is not broken by adversities; and the serpent is set against it, on account of the venom of unbelief. Through the egg the certainty of our hope is figured, because in the egg the perfect offspring is not yet seen, but is hoped for while it is warmed. Against hope he sets the scorpion, whose venomous sting is to be feared from behind; just as the contrary of hope is to look back, since the hope of future things stretches out into what lies before.
57_interl848: the unbelief which the serpent breathed into the first man
57_interl851: because you give not your own things
57_marg866: Being evil. He calls evil the lovers of the world, who give those things which by their own judgment they count good; which are indeed good in their own nature and pertain to the use of this weak life. Or the apostles, who by the merit of election surpassed the goodness of the human race, are still evil in view of the supreme goodness, since they are not yet free from faults, especially in words and in thought, which are commanded to be healed by daily prayers. Or he calls them evil because every creature in the sight of divine goodness is evil, since “no one is good but God”; and yet by participation in divine goodness a rational creature can be made good. The Lord thus promising: “He will give the good Spirit to them that ask him,” so that by participation in the Spirit those who were evil become good, while through the grace of the Spirit they attain faith, hope and charity and the other virtues. Whence Matthew did not say: “He will give the good Spirit to them that ask him,” but “He will give good things to them that ask him,” showing that the Holy Ghost is the fullness of all good things, because through him all good things are ministered.
57_marg867: How much more the Father. A plain comparison. For if a sinful man, still weighed down by frail flesh, does not refuse to give temporal things to children who ask, much more does the heavenly Father bestow in heaven, on his children endowed with his fear and love, goods that never fail.
57_marg868: After the words of preaching which he set before the humble, he also works miracles, so that those who do not believe the preacher may believe when they have seen the miracles. Matthew says that this demoniac was also blind; in him three miracles are done by the Lord: he sees, he speaks, and he is freed from the demon. What was then done bodily in one man is done every day in the conversion of the Gentiles: first the demon is cast out, and all the filth of idolatry, so that they see the light of faith; then mouths that were silent before are loosed to the praise of God.
57_interl853: the scribes and Pharisees, not the simple crowd
57_marg869: Ninus, the king and founder of Nineveh, consecrated a statue to Belus his father, and established divine honours for him; the Chaldeans, receiving the likeness of this image, called him “Bel.” The Palestinians, receiving him, said Baal; the Moabites, Beelphegor. But the Jews, worshippers of the one God, because of the mockery of the Gentiles, called him Beelzebub. For Baal means “man,” and zebub means “fly”; hence Beelzebub, that is, man of flies, or having flies, on account of the filth of the blood which was sacrificed in his temple. The Jews also asserted that the prince of demons dwelt in this image, by whose power they said Jesus cast out demons.
57_marg870: That he might also cause fire to come down from heaven, as in the time of Elias two captains of fifty men were slain by fire from heaven. Or that, against the custom of that land, thunder might be heard in the summer season, rains pour down, and lightnings run, as was done under Samuel. Or they asked for manna from heaven. These signs were not then shown by Christ, because they would likewise have calumniated them, saying that they came from various disturbances of the air. Whence: “But he seeing their thoughts.” The Lord reserved this to himself, to look into thoughts and judge them.
57_marg871: It is proper to the Jews to seek signs. Whence Paul: “The Jews ask for signs; the Gentiles seek wisdom.”
57_marg872: Not to the words but to the thoughts does he answer. In this he gives a sure sign of his power, by which he searches the secrets of hearts. According to the letter it is plain that every kingdom which is solid and firm, if it is divided into parts, is brought to desolation, emptied of its inhabitants; and house falls upon house, and the inhabitants of one house are either oppressed or punished by the family of the other house. How these things tend spiritually he explains when he adds: “And if Satan also be divided against himself.” If I, as you say, cast out devils by the prince of devils, then the kingdom of the devil is divided against itself, and so the power of his malice cannot stand. But if a devil cannot cast out a devil, you falsely say that I cast out devils by the prince of devils. But if he can, as you say, take heed to yourselves, that you go out of his kingdom which is divided, lest you be involved together in its ruin. In what way the Lord casts out demons, so that they may not think him the prince of demons, let them attend to what follows: “And if I by Beelzebub cast out devils, by whom do your children cast them out?” He calls the sons of the Jews “apostles,” who, among the other miracles they had received from the Lord, also drove out demons. This expulsion they assigned not to the devil but to God, being conscious that they had learned nothing of evil arts from the Lord. Therefore, choosing the base and contemptible things of the world, in which there was no crafty malice: “They shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” Or “sons” means exorcists of that people, who, invoking the name of the Lord, drove out demons, as if he said: if the expulsion of demons in them is assigned not to the devil but to God, why should the same work in me not have the same cause? Whence it is added: “Seeking rest; and not finding,” because he who is fed on evil thoughts and acts perceives that all his temptations cease in the minds of the faithful. Then he takes the fullness of all vices. Such spirits, indeed, are called “more wicked” than the devil, because although the devil is evil, those who, by their own merits and impelling vices, are given over to vice, are not only evil but also strive to display the appearance of goodness through hypocrisy, by affecting virtues. “And the last state of that man becomes worse than the first.” It would have been better to be ignorant of the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back.

As a barren fig, abounding in leaves, deserts its owner in hope of fruit, so the teachers of the Synagogue, boasting in their unfruitful works and now in the shade of the law, offer their subjects no example of good work. On the fig, in place of flowers, certain fruits grow which fall off as others grow up; yet some of them remain, which, going out of the wild spirit of the former sap by a milder breeze, are preferred to the rest in appearance and ripeness. So the ancient people of the Synagogue has fallen; in its place, from the fatness of the old religion, the new people of the Church rises up; yet there remained from the people of Israel the apostles, who surpassed the rest.

And the curious mind, as it is skilled in what belongs to another, so much is ignorant of itself. Nor do the words of the one excusing himself differ from the signification of his own vice when he says: “I go to prove them,” because proving is wont to pertain to curiosity.

The Jews, who, rejecting Christ, put the yoke of the law on their necks: where are the five yokes of the ten words, or the five books of the old law. The heretics, who, like Eve with feminine affection, tempt the rigour of faith, and, slipping by slippery ease, aspire to the allurements of false beauty, neglecting the unspoiled beauty of truth. Therefore, after the disdain of the rich, the Lord turns to the Gentiles. He brings in good and bad, that he may increase the good and change the affections of the bad for the better. He invites the poor and the feeble, the blind and the lame, showing that bodily weakness excludes no one from the kingdom, and that one to whom the allurement of sinning is lacking rarely offends, and is more quickly converted to the Lord, who has nothing in the world in which to take delight.

Hence elsewhere: “I am not come to call the just, but sinners.” He says therefore: “there shall be joy in heaven upon one sinner that doth penance, more than upon ninety-nine just who need not penance,” because, as we daily experience, those who have committed no unlawful acts often indulge themselves in lawful things, and do not anxiously pant after heavenly things. And because they are secure, they remain slow to do good; the sinner, on the contrary, usually does the opposite. So there is greater joy over him than over the just man who stands firm; as a leader in battle loves more the soldier who, returning after flight, presses the enemy hard, than the one who never fled nor ever fought bravely. But there are also some just men over whom there is such joy that no penitent can be put before them, who, though they are not conscious of evils in themselves, nevertheless reject lawful things and humble themselves in all things. 57_marg1154: There is a difference between servant, hired man and son. The servant is he who restrains himself from vices from fear of present or future punishment. The hired man is he who refrains from vices out of hope and desire for the kingdom of heaven. The son is he who, kindled with love of the good itself and of the virtues, detests with his whole hatred whatever is contrary to them. Hence the prodigal, when he returned to himself and feared the punishments of hunger, having now become a servant, immediately desired to be a hired man, already thinking of wages. But the father, running to meet him, not content to grant lesser things, having passed quickly through both grades, restored him to the former dignity of sons. And now he makes him think not of the wages of a hired man but of the inheritance of a parent. Hence he does not add what he had intended to say, “make me as one of thy hired servants”, though, having no bread, he had wished to be a hired man; this, after the father’s kiss, he most nobly disdains.

57_marg1165: Jerome. Having followed the justice of the law, he was not subject to the justice of God. For what greater justice is there of God than to pardon penitents? “I have never transgressed thy commandment”: as if it were not transgression to envy another’s salvation or to boast of one’s justice. “I have never transgressed” belongs to a life lived without complaint, and to boasting, not to truth; the father does not consent to it, but restrains it by another reason. “Thou art with me,” by the law by which thou art bound. Not that he had not sinned, but because God by chastising always called him back. Hence: “And if his children forsake my law, and walk not in my judgments: I will visit their iniquities with a rod: and their sins with stripes.” Nor is it strange if he lies to the father who envies his brother, since in judgment too they lie more shamelessly: “Have we not cast out devils in thy name?” “Thou hast never given me,” etc.: the blood of no prophet or priest freed us from the Roman empire, and for the Gentiles glorious blood is shed. “He feasts with his friends, the father being absent”: because always in the field, that is at the end of the world, he will sacrifice the kid, that is Antichrist, and he will be sated with his friends, the demons. Hence it is said: “Thou hast broken the heads of the dragon: thou hast given him to be meat for the people of the Ethiopians”, that is, to those unwilling to be converted you have given him in whom they may delight. “Thou hast killed for him the fatted calf”: he confesses that Christ has come, but through envy he does not wish to be saved. So of the Jew and the Gentile; generally, however, it can be taken of the just man and the sinner. But how does the just man envy his brother, and is not overcome by the father’s correction? But all justice in comparison with God is not justice. Hence Paul: “As many as are perfect.” And elsewhere: “Wretched man that I am! who will deliver me from the body of this death?” Envy falls also on the saints, as the apostles were indignant at the petition of the mother of the sons of Zebedee. Nor is it strange, since this is thought also of the angels: “The stars are not clean in his sight,” and: “Among his angels he found something perverse?” “All my things are thine”: all is referred not always to the whole but to the greater part, as: “All have gone aside, together they are become unprofitable”; “All who came are thieves”; “I am made all things to all men.” All seek what is their own: “all my things are thine”; not the angels, but the law and the prophets; although he has denied nothing to the one whom he urges to eat of the calf.

57_marg1430: Which is called the pasch, etc. The Pasch is named not from passion but “from passing over,” because on that day the destroyer passed through Egypt, or the Lord, delivering his people; by this name it was signified that on this day the Lamb would pass from the world to the Father. Between the Pasch and the unleavened bread there is this difference: the Pasch is called the single day on which the lamb was killed at evening, that is, on the fourteenth day of the first month. The days of unleavened bread were from the fifteenth day of the moon to the twenty-first day of the same month. But the evangelists place indifferently both the day of unleavened bread for the Pasch and the Pasch for the days of unleavened bread. Whence here Luke: “The feast of unleavened bread, which is called the pasch,” because the Pasch was also commanded to be celebrated on the days of unleavened bread. And we, as those making a perpetual Pasch, are always commanded to pass out of this world; after the lamb is sacrificed at evening, seven days of unleavened bread follow, because Christ, having suffered once for us in the fullness of times, has commanded that for the whole time of the age, which is lived out in seven days, we live “with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.”
